claims.text: The degree of local lattice distortion governs high-temperature mechanical strength in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Chemical short-range order governs high-temperature mechanical strength in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The degree of local lattice distortion governs the high-temperature thermoelastic response of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Chemical short-range order governs the high-temperature thermoelastic response of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Changing alloy composition can vary atomic size mismatch and chemical order while overall phase and grain structure are held constant.
Lower atomic size mismatch produces less local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion affects dislocation mobility.
Chemical short-range ordering affects dislocation mobility.
Local lattice distortion and chemical short-range ordering affect elastic stiffness.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases resistance to dislocation movement.
Enhanced lattice distortion alters atomic bonding.
Greater resistance to dislocation movement leads to increased yield strength.
Distortion-induced changes in atomic bonding lead to changes in elastic modulus or thermoelastic recovery.
Alloys engineered for increased lattice distortion will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to lower-distortion controls.
Alloys engineered for increased lattice distortion will have a distinct thermoelastic response relative to lower-distortion controls.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 1000–1600°C when the alloys remain phase-stable without significant transformations or precipitation.
TEM and XRD can be used to quantify the relevant lattice-distortion difference between test and control alloys.
